title: Understanding the landscape of web-based medical misinformation about vaccination
screen_reason: Content analysis of 1,672 US vaccination web pages harvested from search-engine results (mostly Google, 5 results pages deep, 2020). 107 were flagged by trained coders as possibly presenting strictly medical misinformation and 56 were confirmed by a public health expert, giving an exact part/whole share of items classified as misinformation with a stated denominator (R8-compliant).

estimates.country: U.S. (searches run from five U.S. states; SEO data restricted to the US)
estimates.platform: web pages retrieved via Google (mostly), Bing and DuckDuckGo search results
estimates.measure_type: % of vaccination web pages found in search results that were confirmed to present medical misinformation
estimates.value_raw: 56 confirmed of 1,672 catalogued vaccination web pages (56/1672 = 3.3%)
estimates.denominator: 1,672 vaccination web pages in the U.S. catalogued from manual searches (Google, Bing, DuckDuckGo; five results pages deep) for which Ahrefs SEO data were available
estimates.definition: Page flagged by two trained coders as possibly presenting strictly medical misinformation AND confirmed as such by a public health expert; a conservative definition excluding non-medical (e.g. financial) false claims and bare assertions that vaccines are unsafe
estimates.misinfo_def: "We took a conservative approach to defining medical misinformation. For example, simply claiming that vaccines are unsafe was not coded as medical misinformation since different people might have different standards for whether something is safe. ... However, claiming that vaccines are unsafe because they are full of toxins or that vaccines cause autism were classified as medical misinformation."
estimates.source_quote: vaccines or equating vaccination with the biblical “mark of the beast” were not included) and evaluated by a public health expert experienced with vaccine health education. Of these, 56 were confirmed as presenting medical misinfor-
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two trained coders judged each page, differences settled by consensus, after graded training on exemplar blocks of 20/30/50 sites; flagged pages were then verified by a public health expert experienced with vaccine health education, so no page entered the misinformation set on a single judgement. Inter-rater reliability is reported only for the ancillary codes (overarching gist conditional IRR 0.76 / absolute agreement 0.93; narrative 0.72 / 0.96; emotional appeal 0.81 / 0.98) - NO reliability statistic is reported for the medical-misinformation judgement itself.
estimates.moderator_quote: We manually searched the web for information about vaccination on computers void of cookies in private browsing mode to ensure that previous searches would not influence subsequent results. Searches were conducted in 2020 from five U.S. States (in the East, Midwest, and West) on the Bing, DuckDuckGo, and Google search engines. ... For each search, we cataloged vaccination results five Google results pages deep, with a stop rule per search set when no new URLs were found on the first results page.
estimates.notes: The authors never state this percentage; it is the exact part/whole share of two verbatim counts with the same denominator (56 of 1,672), permitted by R8. Denominator is the Ahrefs-covered subset: 2,010 pages catalogued, minus 82 duplicates, minus 107 COVID-but-not-vaccination, minus 149 with no Ahrefs data = 1,672. Note an internal inconsistency in the OCR of Fig. 1: the box "Remove Pages Not Verified as Having Medical Misinformation, Removed N = 81" applied to 107 would leave 26, not the 56 stated in the text and used throughout the Results; I have followed the text (56), and 1,672 = 107 + 1,565 checks out. Search corpus is rank-truncated (five results pages deep), hence denom_selection=curated. Platform coded Google Search because the frame is search results and all traffic/SEO data are Google-based, though Bing and DuckDuckGo were also used. Source quote replaced (it was a multi-sentence join) with the longest contiguous span; the PRISMA-style figure's labels are interleaved with this paragraph line by line, so the quote ends on the line-break hyphen of "misinfor-mation". The denominator sentence, also contiguous, reads: "thus we were able to catalog data for 1672 web pages about vaccination in the U.S. Of these pages,". 56/1672 = 3.3%.

estimates.measure_type: % of vaccination web pages found in search results flagged by trained coders as possibly presenting medical misinformation, before expert verification
estimates.value_raw: 107 flagged of 1,672 catalogued vaccination web pages (107/1672 = 6.4%)
estimates.denominator: 1,672 vaccination web pages in the U.S. catalogued from manual search-engine searches with Ahrefs SEO data

estimates.ground_truth_detail: Trained coders only, deliberately over-inclusive: "All judgments about medical misinformation were made by trained coders who were instructed to flag pages that could possibly contain medical misinformation." No reliability statistic reported for this judgement.
estimates.moderator_quote: All judgments about medical misinformation were made by trained coders who were instructed to flag pages that could possibly contain medical misinformation. Those initial judgments were confirmed by a public health expert. Thus, although some coders produced initial "false alarms" that were identified by public health expert, none of the misinformation pages analyzed here was included without two judgments.
estimates.notes: Broader-definition companion to the 3.3% row: the same denominator, but the numerator is the recall-oriented coder screen before expert adjudication. This is a screening step, not an alternative substantive definition of misinformation, so it is flagged borderline and should NOT be pooled alongside the 3.3% row; it is recorded only because the pair quantifies how much expert verification moves the estimate (6.4% -> 3.3%, i.e. 51 of 107 flags were false alarms). Safe for an adjudicator to drop. Source quote replaced (it was an ellipsis join) with the longest contiguous span; the figure label "Misinformaon" [sic] follows immediately on the same line of the text rendering, which is where the span ends. The sentence continues "misinformation (other kinds of misinformation such as exaggerating the profits pharmaceutical companies make from vaccines or equating vaccination with the biblical 'mark of the beast' were not included) and evaluated by a public health expert experienced with vaccine health education." Denominator sentence: "thus we were able to catalog data for 1672 web pages about vaccination in the U.S. Of these pages,". 107/1672 = 6.4%.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) CONCENTRATION was described but never quantified as a group%/share% pair, so R1 fails: "Table 1 demonstrates that the distribution of pages presenting medical misinformation is heavily skewed with just a few pages accounting for the majority of traffic" and "a relative handful of pages having the lion's share of impact". Table 1 lists monthly traffic for the 13 highest-traffic misinformation pages (2400, 1400, 1300, 933, 797, 137, 98, 87, 81, 50, 44, 41, 39) and the mean over all 56 pages (135.8), from which a top-13 share could be derived, but that would be a cross-category sum I computed, which R8 forbids. (2) Figures cited from elsewhere, excluded by R8: Wolfe et al. (under review) - "websites in search clusters expressing vaccination concerns (N = 531) had significantly more pages with medical misinformation, 7.2% than other clusters (N = 667,) with 2.1%"; and Caldarelli et al. (2021) - "the impact of disreputable Twitter posts about COVID-19 in Italy exceeded 20% in conservative communities, with 96% of all disreputable URLs shared by political Twitter groups coming from right- and center right-wing communities". (3) Shares computed inside the misinformation-only sample that are NOT falsity measures and so are not R3 rows: 54.5% of misinformation pages had at least one organic Google visitor/month (vs 77.4% of non-misinformation pages); 22.2% had at least one backlink (vs 8.1%); 32.7% had an overarching gist (vs 23.2%); 7.7% presented narratives (vs 12.1%); 17.3% made emotional appeals (vs 6.0%). These describe page characteristics and traffic, not prevalence of false content. (4) Coh-Metrix scores (FKGL 11.494, GIS -0.234, etc.) are readability/inference scale scores, not shares, and not truth judgements, so no QUALITY row was created. (5) Mean traffic (135.8 misinformation vs 1062.8 non-misinformation visits/month) and mean backlinks (805.0 vs 13,000.1) are per-page intensities of attention, not of misinformation exposure, so no per_capita_intensity row.

rob.design: Cross-sectional content analysis, 2020. Manual searches from five US states on Google (mostly), Bing and DuckDuckGo, in private browsing with no cookies, using search terms starting with every letter of the alphabet; results catalogued five Google results pages deep with a stop rule when a search returned no new URLs. Flow: 2,010 pages catalogued -> 82 duplicates removed -> 107 COVID-but-not-vaccination removed -> 1,821 URLs submitted to Ahrefs -> 149 without SEO data removed -> 1,672 analysed. 107 flagged as possibly containing medical misinformation by two trained coders (differences settled by consensus, staged training on exemplar blocks), of which 56 confirmed by a public health expert. Reliability reported only for the ancillary codes (gist conditional IRR 0.76 / absolute agreement 0.93; narrative 0.72 / 0.96; emotional appeal 0.81 / 0.98); none reported for the misinformation judgement. Traffic, backlinks and keywords from Ahrefs proprietary estimates, not platform-supplied data. Authors' own stated limitations: text-only (no video or dynamic social media), a snapshot in time, possible bias in the initial searches, and a conservative definition that may miss some misinformation pages.
rob.item6_quote: We took a conservative approach to defining medical misinformation. For example, simply claiming that vaccines are unsafe was not coded as medical misinformation since different people might have different standards for whether something is safe. Falsely claiming that pharmaceutical companies make most of their money from vaccines was not coded as medical misinformation since the misinformation is of a financial rather than medical nature. However, claiming that vaccines are unsafe because they are full of toxins or that vaccines cause autism were classified as medical misinformation.
rob.item10_quote: thus we were able to catalog data for 1672 web pages about vaccination in the U.S. Of these pages, 107 were identified as possibly presenting strictly medical misinformation ... and evaluated by a public health expert experienced with vaccine health education. Of these, 56 were confirmed as presenting medical misinformation.
